commit.message:
DeepSeek: the EXL3 lend and the DMA read-back of host-summed pieces opt-in (MAYA_DS4_EXL3_LEND=1, DS4_AR_BACK_DMA=1), the lend never on one GPU (#691)

Neither has run on our machines: there is no DeepSeek EXL3 pack on them, and the DMA read-back needs a
tensor-parallel group of 5+ members and a CUDA 12.5+ build. Both stay as the pull request wrote them, off
until measured here. The lend also refuses to load a layer split whose layers keep too few recent slots for
the chunk, where the same setup loaded before, and the pull request's own note says lent buffers gave wrong
answers on one GPU: the lend now needs two GPUs or more even when asked for.

DeepSeek: long prompts - restore points near the end kept in one read, a chunk streams only the experts it picks, EXL3 chunk buffers lent from the expert cache, host-summed pieces read back by DMA (#691)

Squash of the pull request's 9 commits:

- DeepSeek: a prompt's restore points near its end kept in one read (MAYA_DS4_MARKS_INSIDE; a read from token 0
  still stops at a shared start, #607; a tail point taken on the way costs no stop, so #668's tail cost counts only
  the reads that stop at it); maya-ds4 --marks-check compares the two reads
- DeepSeek on CUDA: a short chunk (up to DS4_SKIP_UNPICKED_ROWS, 1536) streams only the experts it picks - the same
  slots, batches and summing order
- DeepSeek on CUDA: a device with a shallow ring skips unpicked experts on every chunk
- maya-ds4: --ids @FILE reads the ids from a file (a long prompt's are more than one argument may hold)
- DeepSeek: a group whose chunk sums the host makes pins no F32 rows for the copy engines' sums
- DeepSeek: a chunk that skips unpicked experts reads their picks at pv_n (copy_ahead read them at n_slots + j once
  VRAM slots were lent)
- DeepSeek EXL3: a prompt's chunk buffers lent from the expert cache's recent slots (MAYA_DS4_EXL3_LEND;
  DS4_CHECK_LEND=1 compares each lent slot before and after)
- DeepSeek: a chunk's host-summed pieces read back by DMA behind a stream wait (DS4_AR_BACK_DMA; CUDA 12.5+, the
  kernels as before where the driver refuses the wait)
- DeepSeek EXL3: a lending GPU's layer that every expert fitted keeps one in RAM, so it has slots to lend

docs/SETTINGS.md: long prompts on two tensor-parallel groups (--tp 4 + DS4_SPLIT, a setting, not a default).
DS4_RUN_TRACE=1: each device's timeline of a run of chunks.

maya-ds4: the link measured on the legacy stream, and one expert a batch on a slow link (#609)

Since v1.1.39 the prompt ring is sized by each GPU's host link, timed at load with four 32 MB copies.
They ran on a non-blocking stream made for the measurement and destroyed after it. On 2x CMP 170HX
(PCIe Gen2 x16 + x4) that left decode about 20% slower for the whole run with --dspark none (10% with
DSpark on), even with the ring size set by hand and the result unused. Timing the same copies on the
legacy stream removed the loss and measured the same bandwidth. The copies and events now run there,
as the other load copies do, and no stream is made for the measurement.

The ring rule: a link that takes 1 ms or more for one expert now gets one expert a batch. On that
rig's Gen2 x16 card (9 MB experts, 6.2 GB/s) one a batch read 4K-32K prompts 2-3.5% faster than the
6 of ~10 ms. Faster links keep ~10 ms a batch: a V100 on PCIe 3 x16 still picks the same 60 slots
(396 MB).

On one V100 (Maya-XS) the measured link, the ring and decode are unchanged within run-to-run noise. The
loss itself did not show there, nor in a stream / copy-engine probe on an RTX 3050. The reporter's
rig measured both changes.

DeepSeek GGUF tensor parallel: a member reads only its own gate / up rows of an expert read from the files - prompts no longer pay for a whole blob read and half of it moved on the CPU per member (#670)

With the MXFP4/GGUF experts read in place (more of them than the RAM keeps), each tensor parallel member staged
an expert by reading the whole blob from the file and then moving its half of the gate / up rows and its blocks
of the down within the staging slot: about 1.5 blobs of CPU copies per member, where the layer split copies one
blob per expert - on a CPU with few cores that also serves the page-cache reads this became the prompt's limit.
Now the member's gate / up rows are read straight to their place (the same file bytes the blob held at rows
[ff0, ff0 + ffn)) and the down is read whole and cut in place as before: about 0.8 blob per member.

Tested on 2x V100 pinned to 6 cores (12 threads), Maya-XS with the experts in place (--mmap-experts on,
--vram-experts 0.1, 131072 context, no drafting), 8.7K-token prompts, builds interleaved main / this / main /
this (6 starts each): prompts in 0.66-0.70x of main's time, about the --tp 1 time; decode unchanged.  The staged
bytes are the blob's own rows by construction; first-token logprobs agree within main's own run-to-run spread on
this uneven split.  Jupiter ctest: the same results as main.

DeepSeek: a GPU too small for its layers' dense weights fails at the start with what it needs, instead of a cudaMalloc error part way into the load

The dense weights (attention, the shared experts, the head) always stay in VRAM - the CPU lane and
--vram-experts move only the routed experts - so on a card whose free memory cannot hold them the load could
only end in a cudaMalloc failure.  Before anything loads, each device whose layers are whole (not a tensor
parallel member's part) is checked: short, the start ends with the card's free memory, what its layers' dense
weights need, and what to do (a GPU with about that much VRAM plus room for the caches, more GPUs to split the
layers across, or closing other programs on the GPU).  Maya-XS on an 8 GB RTX 3050: "CUDA0 has 8.07 GB free of
8.22 GB, but the dense weights of layers 0-39 and the head need 8.56 GB on it ..." in a few seconds.

MiniMax: a routing id outside the experts ends the request with an error that says where, instead of an access violation in the per-expert tables (#672)

The router's kernel leaves 0x7fffffff where a token's logits are NaN (no expert compares better), and the host
indexed its per-expert counters and CPU-lane records with the ids it read back - the two fault sites the
Windows report disassembled (a counter at layer * n_exp + id, a 24-byte record by id).  The ids are now
checked where the host reads them (the window, the token and the GGUF paths): a bad one fails the request with
the layer, the id and the last CUDA error.  It does not explain why the logits were NaN there; it turns a silent
crash into a line that does.  Built on Linux (V100) and Windows (compile check); no Windows NVIDIA GPU to run it.

GLM --prefill auto: a chunk too short for the prestage ring no longer passes the ring's test - the largest chunk with a part of the ring wins over 768 tokens with none (#673)

The auto search bisects the chunk on the 256-token grid for the largest chunk that leaves the whole prestage
ring, then one that leaves 16 slots of it.  A chunk under 1024 tokens carves no ring, so it "passed" either
test and the test was not monotonic: on a card whose pool could not hold the whole ring beside a 1024-token
chunk, the search settled on 768 tokens with no ring at all.  Those tests now start at 1024.

Reproduced on a V100 capped to the reporter's expert-pool room (Maya-S24, 262144 context, KV streaming,
RAM-resident): 768-token chunks before, 2560 after (with a 19-slot ring) - the same chunk an explicit
--prefill 10240 is halved to there; a 19K-token prompt reads 3.4x faster, a 3.9K one 3.1x.  With more room the
choice is unchanged (10240 / 32768 with the whole ring).

An idle Maya wakes far less: the engines' CPU-lane threads back off and sleep on a gate a request's line wakes, the setup screen and the hardware sampler slow down when nothing runs (#685)

Measured idle (one V100 box, a minute or more after the last request): DeepSeek's CPU-lane thread woke 12,500 times a
second and held 4-12% of a core (it slept 20 us for ever); GLM's polled every 2 ms (468 wakeups a second, ~1.5%); the
setup screen's main thread took ~3.8% of a core (Textual laid the whole screen out for the card's clock and the
dashboard's banner every second); the hardware sampler and its NVML process ~0.9%.

- Engines: DeepSeek's service thread gets the stages GLM's already had (spin through a decode, then 0.1 ms and 2 ms
  sleeps), and both sleep on a gate (idle_gate.hpp) after 60 s without a request, 100 ms at a time,
  ~10 wakeups a second. The thread that reads the engine's input pokes the gate at each line, so the next request
  finds the thread awake before its first route. MAYA_GLM_SERVICE_DEEP_S/_MS, MAYA_DS4_SERVICE_IDLE_MS/DEEP_S/_MS
  (0 = the old behaviour / never); docs/SETTINGS.md.
- Setup screen (maya.py / ./maya.sh): the card's timer ticks once a second when only the clock moves, the events are
  looked for 4 times a second when quiet, a banner is drawn when it changes, and a new reading of the dashboard's
  boxes is drawn without a layout of the whole screen unless a box changed shape (and every tenth reading).
- Server: the hardware sampler pauses 3 s (not 1) while no request runs and nothing has read /metrics for 15 s; a
  read, a request or touch() brings the second back at once, and the series keep their second spacing.

Idle after: DeepSeek engine 12.6% -> 0.3% -> 0 of a core, GLM engine 1.5-1.8% -> 0.02%, setup screen main thread
about half, mock server 0.9% -> 0.25%. GLM first-token times after 65 s of quiet unchanged (747/506/490/468 ms before,
584/485/485/465 after). DeepSeek's on this shared box varied from 0.8 to 6 s run to run with other jobs' RAM use.

Setup no longer calls a discrete NVIDIA card without Resizable BAR "shared with the system": CUDA's integrated attribute decides, and a card that reports its memory is discrete (#671)

A small memory BAR (256 MiB on an RTX A4000 or a Quadro P400 without Resizable BAR) was taken as proof that the GPU's
memory is the system's RAM. The setup now asks the driver (CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_INTEGRATED, the attribute the engine
asks too) for the cards with a small BAR; where the driver cannot be asked, a small-BAR card counts as unified only
when nvidia-smi reports no memory size for it (a GB10 says N/A, a discrete card gives its VRAM).

A setting the engines read only as MAYA_X now works from a config's "env" under either name: the engine and the server get both names (#686)

env_in() gives a loaded config its settings under the older name only, and the engine was started with exactly that, so
every getenv("MAYA_...") (MAYA_DS4_READ_ORDER, MAYA_DS4_INPLACE_TRIM_*, MAYA_EXPERT_*, MAYA_MM3_*, ...) saw nothing.
child_env() now puts each config setting into the engine's environment under both names (as it already did for
Metal), apply_server_env() does the same for the server's own settings (and also takes MAYA_QUEUE_PING_S,
MAYA_UPDATE_CHECK and MAYA_PACK_TEMPLATE, which only the shell reached), and the dashboard's Qwen RAM-tier and GLM
KV-window readers find the setting under either name. The test lists every MAYA_ name the engine sources read and
checks each reaches the engine from a config on disk, plus a started child that reads one.

Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next (CYBER-FROST): pictures on the GPU of an 8 GB card too - the encoder may borrow the whole expert cache, then the draft layer's experts

Nothing decodes while the vision encoder reads a picture, and refilling the cache needs no slot (the experts are copied
straight from RAM), so the engine no longer keeps the first 128 slots back: it lends as much of the cache as the
encoder needs, all of it if need be. When even the whole cache is short, the draft layer's 512 experts on that GPU
follow: they now live in the same kind of lendable memory (the virtual memory code moved out of the expert cache into
LendableArena, which both use), are given back in 64 MiB pieces after the cache, and are read again from their file
when the memory comes back, at the same addresses. VLEND measures the free VRAM each time, lends only what is short,
answers ERR when even both cannot cover it, and logs what the encoder finds free. At start the engine says which of
the three it will use - free VRAM, the cache, the cache and the draft layer - or, when even all of it cannot hold the
encoder, that the encoder runs on the CPU and why. Only a drafter on the encoder's GPU is lendable (a layer split keeps
it on its last GPU, unchanged); the HIP build and GPUs without the virtual memory API keep lending only free VRAM.

Uranus (RTX 3050 8 GB, --max-context 32768): the 1.36 GB encoder used to fall back to the CPU (0.20 GB free + 0.60 GB
lendable); it now runs on the GPU with the whole cache (1.03 GB) and 0.22-0.29 GB of the draft layer's experts lent,
1.52 GB free when it starts. Both test pictures answered correctly; reading a picture (the request less its prompt and
answer) takes about 3.6x less time than with the CPU encoder, the whole request about 25% less (most of it is the
698-token prompt). The memory comes back in about 1.2 s per request (cache refill ~1.0 s, draft experts ~0.2 s). Greedy
text answers (adaptive tier and suffix drafts off) after two pictures are byte for byte the ones before them; decode
speed after the pictures is the same as before (within 1%). A smaller encoder budget for small cards was checked and
left out: 512 image tokens would save only 86 MiB (6%) and the encoder needs at least 1024 for grounding.
expert_cache_lend_test also lends the whole cache and checks a plain arena (tail lent, head kept, same address).
